1 Setting up R Packages

library(tidyverse) # Data Processing in R
library(mosaic) # Our workhorse for stats, sampling
library(janitor) # Data Cleaning
library(skimr) # Good to Examine data
library(ggformula) # Formula interface for graphs

# load the NHANES data library
library(NHANES)
library(infer)

  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +

      panel.widths = unit(11, "cm"),

        size = 8

        size = 6
      ),

        family = "Alegreya",
        size = 8
      )

      caption = element_text(
        family = "Alegreya",
        size = 6
      ),
      caption.position = "plot"
    )
}

2 What is a Population?

A population is a collection of individuals or observations we are interested in. This is also commonly denoted as a study population in science research, or a target audience in design. We mathematically denote the population’s size using upper-case N.

A population parameter is some numerical summary about the population that is unknown but you wish you knew. For example, when this quantity is a mean like the mean height of all Bangaloreans, the population parameter of interest is the population mean \(\mu_{pop}\).

A census is an exhaustive enumeration or counting of all N individuals in the population. We do this in order to compute the population parameter’s value exactly. Of note is that as the number N of individuals in our population increases, conducting a census gets more expensive (in terms of time, energy, and money).

Important Parameters

Populations Parameters are usually indicated by Greek Letters.

3 What is a Sample?

Sampling is the act of collecting a small subset from the population, which we generally do when we can’t perform a census. We mathematically denote the sample size using lower case n, as opposed to upper case N which denotes the population’s size. Typically the sample size n is much smaller than the population size N. Thus sampling is a much cheaper alternative than performing a census.

A sample statistic, also known as a point estimate, is a summary statistic like a mean or standard deviation that is computed from a sample.

NoteWhy do we sample?

Because we cannot conduct a census ( not always ) — and sometimes we won’t even know how big the population is — we take samples. And we still want to do useful work for/with the population, after estimating its parameters, an act of generalizing from sample to population. So the question is, can we estimate useful parameters of the population, using just samples? Can point estimates serve as useful guides to population parameters?

This act of generalizing from sample to population is at the heart of statistical inference.

ImportantAn Alliterative Mnemonic

NOTE: there is an alliterative mnemonic here: Samples have Statistics; Populations have Parameters.

4 Population Parameters and Sample Statistics

Parameters and Statistics
Population Parameter Sample Statistic
Mean \(\mu\) \(\bar{x}\)
Standard Deviation \(\sigma\) s
Proportion p \(\hat{p}\)
Correlation \(\rho\) r
Slope (Regression) \(\beta_1\) \(b_1\)

Some examples:

NoteQuestion

Q.1. What is the mean commute time for workers in a particular city?

A.1. The parameter is the mean commute time \(\mu\) for a population containing all workers who work in the city. We estimate it using \(\bar{x}\), the mean of the random sample of people who work in the city.

NoteQuestion

Q.2. What is the correlation between the size of dinner bills and the size of tips at a restaurant?

A.2. The parameter is \(\rho\) , the correlation between bill amount and tip size for a population of all dinner bills at that restaurant. We estimate it using r, the correlation from a random sample of dinner bills.

NoteQuestion

Q.3. How much difference is there in the proportion of 30 to 39-year-old residents who have only a cell phone (no land line phone) compared to 50 to 59-year-olds in the country?

A.3. The population is all citizens of the country, and the parameter is \(p_1 - p_2\), the difference in proportion of 30 to 39-year-old residents who have only a cell phone (\(p_1\)) and the proportion with the same property among all 50 to 59-year olds (\(p_2\)). We estimate it using (\(\hat{p_1} - \hat{p_2}\)), the difference in sample proportions computed from random samples taken from each group.

Sample statistics vary and in the following we will estimate this uncertainty and decide how reliable they might be as estimates of population parameters.

5 So What do We Want?

Let us define the purpose we have in mind:

  • We want to estimate the population parameters, such as the population mean \(\mu\) and the population standard deviation \(\sigma\).
  • We want to take just one sample from the population, and compute the sample statistics such as the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) and the sample standard deviation \(s\).
  • (Because that is all we can afford, let us say).
  • We want to be sure that estimates from the sample are not very much off from the population parameters.
  • And we want to know how to quantify that uncertainty.

To achieve this purpose, we need a certain amount of theoretical justification. Let us now dig into those systematically.

Let us create a NHANES (sub)-dataset without duplicated IDs and only adults and select the Height variable:

Show the Code
NHANES_adult <-
  NHANES %>%
  distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(Age >= 18) %>%
  select(Height) %>%
  drop_na(Height)
NHANES_adult
ImportantAn “Assumed” Population

We will now onwards treat this single-variable dataset as our Population. So this is our population, with appropriate population parameters such as pop_mean = \(\mu\), and pop_sd = \(\sigma\).

Let us calculate the population parameters for the Height data from our “assumed” population:

# NHANES_adult is assumed population
pop_mean <- mosaic::mean(~Height, data = NHANES_adult)
pop_sd <- mosaic::sd(~Height, data = NHANES_adult)
pop_mean
[1] 168.3497
pop_sd
[1] 10.15705

Let us now start our sampling game!

6.1 Sampling

Now, we will sample ONCE from the Height variable. Let us take a sample of sample size n = 50. We will compare sample statistics with population parameters on the basis of this ONE sample of n = 50:

Show the Code
set.seed(12345) # for reproducibility
sample_50 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 50) %>%
  select(Height)
sample_50
sample_mean_50 <- mean(~Height, data = sample_50)
sample_mean_50
# Plotting the histogram of this sample
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())
sample_50 %>%
  gf_histogram(~Height, bins = 10) %>%
  gf_vline(
    xintercept = ~sample_mean_50,
    color = "purple"
  ) %>%
  gf_vline(
    xintercept = ~pop_mean,
    colour = "black"
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("label",
    y = 7, x = pop_mean - 8,
    label = "Population Mean",
    color = "black"
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("label",
    y = 7, x = sample_mean_50 + 8,
    label = "Sample Mean", color = "purple"
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("curve",
    x = sample_mean_50 + 8, y = 6.5,
    xend = sample_mean_50 + 1, yend = 2,
    curvature = -0.2, color = "purple",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm"))
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("curve",
    x = pop_mean - 8, y = 6.5,
    xend = pop_mean - 1, yend = 2,
    curvature = 0.2, color = "black", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm"))
  ) %>%
  gf_labs(
    y = "Frequency",
    title = "Distribution and Mean of a Single Sample",
    subtitle = "Sample Size = 50"
  )
[1] 170.094

A Single Sample of size 50.

6.2 Repeated Samples and Sample Means

OK, so the sample_mean_50(\(\bar{x}\)) is not too far from the pop_mean (\(\mu\)). Is this always true, i.e. for any sample?

Let us check: we will create 500 repeated samples, each of size 50. And calculate their mean as the sample statistic, giving us a data frame containing 500 sample means (\(\bar{x}\)-s). We will then see if all these 500 means lie close to the pop_mean(\(\mu\)):

Show the Code
sample_50_500 <- do(500) * {
  sample(NHANES_adult, size = 50) %>%
    select(Height) %>% # drop sampling related column "orig.id"
    summarise(
      sample_mean = mean(Height),
      sample_sd = sd(Height),
      sample_min = min(Height),
      sample_max = max(Height)
    )
}
sample_50_500 <-
  sample_50_500 %>%
  select(index = .index, sample_min, sample_max, sample_mean, sample_sd)
sample_50_500
dim(sample_50_500)
[1] 500   5
Show the Code
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

sample_50_500 %>%
  gf_point(index ~ sample_mean,
    color = "purple",
    title = "Sample Means are close to the Population Mean",
    subtitle = "Sample Means are Random!",
    caption = "Grey lines represent our 500 samples"
  ) %>%
  gf_segment(
    index + index ~ sample_min + sample_max,
    color = "grey",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.3,
    ylab = "Sample Index (1-500)",
    xlab = "Sample Means"
  ) %>%
  gf_vline(
    xintercept = ~pop_mean,
    color = "black"
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("label",
    y = -25, x = pop_mean,
    label = "Population Mean",
    color = "black"
  )

##

sample_50_500 %>%
  gf_point(index ~ sample_sd,
    color = "purple",
    title = "Sample SDs are close to the Population SD",
    subtitle = "Sample SDs are Random!",
  ) %>%
  gf_vline(
    xintercept = ~pop_sd,
    color = "black"
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("label",
    y = -25, x = pop_sd,
    label = "Population SD",
    color = "black"
  ) %>%
  gf_refine(lims(x = c(4, 16))) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Sample SDs", y = "Sample Index (1-500)")
NoteSample Means and Sample SDs are a Random Variables!!1

The sample_means (the \(\bar{x}\)-s, purple dots Figure 2 (a)) are all generally in the vicinity of the pop_mean (\(\mu\), vertical black line). And since they are themselves random because the samples are random, they will have their own distribution, with a mean and sd too, over all the 500 sample-means.

And the sample_sd(the \(s\)-s) are also random (see Figure 2 (b)) and have their own distribution, around the pop_sd (\(\sigma\)).2. This distribution of the sample-sds will also have its own mean and sd too !!

Are you confused yet? Hold tight! 😱 😱 😱 😱

6.3 Distribution of Sample-Means

So now let’s plot the distribution of these 500 sample-means themselves, called a distribution of sample-means. We will also plot the position of the population mean pop_mean parameter \(\mu\), the mean of the Height variable.

Note

WHY? Because we want to see how the sample-means are distributed around the population mean, and how they compare with the population distribution itself.

6.4 Deriving the Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

  • We see in the Figure 3 (a) above that the distribution of sample-means is centered around the pop_mean \(\mu\). ( Mean of the sample means = pop_mean \(\mu\)!! 😱)
  • And from Figure 3 (b) that the “spread” aka sd of the distribution of sample means is within than population itself. Well within ! Curiouser and curiouser!
  • But exactly how much is it? And what is the kind of distribution?
  • Why are we interested? Any single sample needs to give us an estimate for pop_mean \(\mu\). And it had better be good, with small standard deviation.
  • And does the sample size matter? Does the sample mean distribution change if we take a larger sample?

From the histograms we learn that the sample-means are normally distributed around the population mean. This feels intuitively right because when we sample from the population, many values will be close to the population mean, and values far away from the mean will be increasingly scarce.

Let us calculate the means of the 4 sample-mean-distributions:

mean(~mean, data = samples_08_1000) # Mean of means!!!;-0
mean(~mean, data = samples_16_1000)
mean(~mean, data = samples_32_1000)
mean(~mean, data = samples_64_1000)
pop_mean
[1] 168.2391
[1] 168.2224
[1] 168.3131
[1] 168.3706
[1] 168.3497

All are nearly identical, and also pretty close to the population mean !!! So regardless of sample size, we get an estimate of the pop_mean from the mean of a sample! Whoo-Hoo!!! But how good can the estimate be? How much uncertainty is there in this estimate?

For that, we need to look at the standard deviations of the 4 sampling-mean distributions:

\[ \Large{sd_i = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma^{1000}_{k} {[{mean_k} - \overline{mean_k}}]^2}{n_i}}}~, i = 1...4 \]

We take the sum of all squared differences from the mean in a sample. If we divide this sum-of-squared-differences by the sample length \(n\), we get a sort of average squared difference, or per-capita squared error from the mean, which is called the variance.

Taking the square root gives us an average error, which we would call, of course, the standard deviation.

pop_sd
sd(~mean, data = samples_08_1000)
sd(~mean, data = samples_16_1000)
sd(~mean, data = samples_32_1000)
sd(~mean, data = samples_64_1000)
[1] 10.15705
[1] 3.70518
[1] 2.635219
[1] 1.874483
[1] 1.333163

These are also decreasing steadily with sample size. How are they related to the pop_sd?

pop_sd
pop_sd / sqrt(8)
pop_sd / sqrt(16)
pop_sd / sqrt(32)
pop_sd / sqrt(64)
[1] 10.15705
[1] 3.591058
[1] 2.539262
[1] 1.795529
[1] 1.269631
ImportantSD of Sample-mean-distribution reduces with \(1/sqrt(n)\)

As we can see, the standard deviations of the sampling-mean-distributions is inversely proportional to the square root of lengths of the sample. Which means that as we increase the sample size of our planned single sample, the standard deviation of the sample-mean-distribution decreases, and so does the uncertainty in our estimate of the pop_mean!

NoteCentral Limit Theorem

Now we have enough to state the Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

  • the sample-means are normally distributed around the population mean. So any mean of a single sample is a good, unbiased estimate for the pop_mean.

    \[ \Large{\bar{x} \sim pop.mean } \tag{1}\]

  • the sample-mean distributions are centered around the pop_mean and have a standard deviation that is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size..

    \[ \Large{s \sim \frac{pop.sd}{sqrt(n)} } \tag{2}\]

  • This is regardless of the distribution of the population itself.3

This theorem underlies all our procedures and techniques for statistical inference, as we shall see.

Understanding the Central Limit Theorem

7 The Standard Error

Consider once again the standard deviations in each of the sample-mean-distributions that we have generated. As we saw, these are smaller than the pop_sd \(\sigma\), and decrease with sample size:

sd = pop_sd/sqrt(sample_size) where sample-size4 here is one of c(8, 16, 32, 64).

Important

We reserve the term Standard Deviation for the population sd, \(\sigma\), and name this computed standard deviation of the sample-mean-distributions as the Standard Error. This statistic derived from the sample-mean-distribution will help us infer our population parameters with a precise estimate of the uncertainty involved.

\[ \Large{Standard\ Error\ \pmb {se} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt[]{n}}}\\ \tag{3}\]

However, we don’t normally know the pop_sd!! So now what?? So is this chicken and egg??

8 Back to One Sample!!

Remember, we are poor, and lazy. Let us take SINGLE SAMPLES of each size, as we normally would:

set.seed(1963)
sample_08 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 8)
sample_16 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 16)
sample_32 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 32)
sample_64 <- mosaic::sample(NHANES_adult, size = 64)
##
pop_sd
sd(~Height, data = sample_08)
sd(~Height, data = sample_16)
sd(~Height, data = sample_32)
sd(~Height, data = sample_64)
[1] 10.15705
[1] 7.684481
[1] 13.49193
[1] 10.73322
[1] 10.1388
WarningDistribution of Sample SDs

As we saw at the start of this module, the sample-means are distributed around the pop_mean, AND it appears that the sample-sds are also distributed around the pop_sd!

However, the sample-sd distribution is not Gaussian (because an sd can never be negative), and the sample_sd is also not an unbiased estimate for the pop_sd. However, when the sample size \(n\) is large (\(n >= 30\)), the sample-sd distribution approximates the Gaussian, and the bias is small.

And so, in the same way, we approximate the pop_sd with the sd of a single sample of the same length. Hence the Standard Error can be computed from a single sample as:

\[ \boxed{\Large{Standard\ Error\ \pmb {se} \sim \frac{sample.sd}{\sqrt[]{n}}}} \tag{4}\]

With these, the Standard Errors(SE) evaluate to:

pop_sd
sd(~Height, data = sample_08) / sqrt(8)
sd(~Height, data = sample_16) / sqrt(16)
sd(~Height, data = sample_32) / sqrt(32)
sd(~Height, data = sample_64) / sqrt(64)
[1] 10.15705
[1] 2.716874
[1] 3.372984
[1] 1.897383
[1] 1.26735

Why are we concerned with Standard Errors(SE)? Because they are the uncertainty in our sample-mean estimates of the population mean. And when we want to be more certain, we need to reduce the SE and therefore…make our sample larger. Design hack!

9 Confidence intervals

When we work with samples, we want to be able to speak with a certain degree of confidence about the population mean, based on the evaluation of one sample mean, not a large number of them. Given that sample-means are normally distributed around the pop_mean \(\mu\), we can say that:

  • \(68\%\) of all possible sample-mean-s lie within \(\pm 1* SE\) of the population mean;
  • \(95 \%\) of all possible sample-mean-s lie within \(\pm 2 * SE\) of the population mean.
  • These two multiplier-constants \(\pm 1\) and \(\pm 2\) are the z-scores from the z-distribution we saw earlier5.
Show the Code
set.seed(42) # Not a good idea always!
###
mosaic::xqnorm(
  p = c((1 - 0.68) / 2, 1 - (1 - 0.68) / 2),
  return = c("plot"), verbose = F,
  system = "gg", pattern = "rings",
  alpha = 0.5, colour = "black",
) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Z-score (Increments of SE)", title = "68% Confidence Intervals") %>%
  gf_refine(scale_x_continuous(breaks = -4:4))

  alpha = 0.5, colour = "black"
) %>%
  gf_labs(x = "Z-score (Increments of SE)", title = "95% Confidence Intervals") %>%

TeachingDemos::ci.examp(mean.sim = 100, sd = 2, n = 50, reps = 50, method = "z")

In Figure 6 (c), we see that \(95\%\) confidence intervals straddle the population mean shown in black, almost always. For a particular sample with \(\bar{x} === 100\), the vertical red lines show the confidence interval derived from that sample. One sample in 50 has missed it and is shown in pink.

So:

  • Every sample we could take sets up a Gaussian distribution for the estimate of the pop_mean \(\mu\). (Which is sample_mean \(\bar{x}\) in this case.)
  • Each sample will have a different sample_mean \(\bar{x}\), and therefore the distribution curves, being centred on sample_mean would move to the right or to the left.
  • Each such sample distribution sets up a Confidence Interval.
  • We expect that 95% out of all the samples will setup a Confidence Interval that contains the pop_mean \(\mu\).
  • THEREFORE, any one of all those samples is good enough and all that we need!!!

11 CLT Workflow

Thus if we want to estimate a population mean:

  • we take one random sample from the population of length \(n\)
  • we calculate the mean from the sample_mean \(\bar{x}\)
  • we calculate the sample_sd \(s\)
  • we calculate the Standard Error as \(\frac{s}{\sqrt[]{n}}\)
  • we calculate 95% confidence intervals for the population parameter based on the formula \(CI_{95\%}= \bar{} \pm 2*SE\).
  • So finally, \[ \boxed{\Large{\mu \sim \bar{x} \pm 2.0 * \frac{s}{\sqrt[]{n}}}} \tag{5}\]

12 CLT Assumptions

  • Population Standard Deviation \(\sigma\) is known;
  • Sample is of “decent length” \(n >= 30\);
  • Therefore sample histogram is Gaussian.

When these are violated, as with small sample sizes, or with unknown population sds, we need to use the t-distribution instead of the z-distribution to calculate confidence intervals. The t-distribution is a family of distributions that are similar to the Gaussian, but have heavier tails. This leads to slightly wider Confidence Intervals being computed.

14 Wait, But Why?

  • We want to take one sample from a population and use it to make inferences about population parameters
  • We compute a statistic from the sample, i.e. a mean
  • We want to be able to say how accurate it is, i.e. state its mean and standard deviation, and the relative probability of how probable the statistic could be
  • Relative probabilities, means, and standard deviations are only possible to calculate if we have many means, and therefore, many samples!!
  • So we, as frequentist people, pretend we can take many samples and calculate the mean of the means and the standard deviation of the means (Now called standard error), and the relative probability of a the calculated statistic
  • These tell us how the means are distributed and how accurate the mean-mean can be
  • Since standard error uses the (unknown and unknowable) population sd, we approximate that by sample sd
  • Since Standard Error decreases with sample size, we need to make our sample of adequate size.( \(n=30\) seems appropriate in most cases. Why?)
  • And we do not have to worry about the distribution of the population. It need not be normal/Gaussian/Bell-shaped !!
